questions.prompt: R is an **interpreted** language. What does that mean?
choices: It runs code one line at a time, translating and running each line as it goes.
It translates the whole program into machine code before any of it runs.
It can only run code that has been knitted.
It translates R code into English.
questions.explain: An interpreter is like a live translator at a conference, translating sentence by sentence. A compiler is like a book translator, who translates the whole book first.

questions.prompt: In the translation analogy, which one is like a **compiler**?
choices: A book translator who translates the whole book before anyone reads it
A live translator who translates a speech sentence by sentence
A reader who skips to the last page
questions.explain: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs. R is interpreted, so it works like the live translator.

questions.prompt: A file has three chunks: `day <- 1`, `day <- 2`, and `day <- 3`. You run the third chunk, then the first. What does `day` hold now?
questions.explain: R keeps whichever value it was given most recently. The order you ran the chunks matters, not their order in the file.

questions.prompt: Knitting runs every chunk from the top of the file in a fresh R session.
questions.explain: That's why a file that only works when chunks are run out of order fails to knit.

questions.prompt: Which RStudio command checks that your file works from a clean start, the same way knitting does?
choices: Run > Restart R and Run All Chunks
questions.explain: Restart R and Run All Chunks clears memory and reruns the file from the top. If it works, your file will knit.

questions.prompt: Where in RStudio do you check the current value of every variable?
questions.explain: The Environment pane always shows what R is holding right now.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a **package** and a **library**?
choices: A package is a bundle of code; a library is the folder where installed packages are stored.
A library is a bundle of code; a package is the folder where libraries are stored.
They are two names for exactly the same thing.
Packages come from CRAN; libraries come from GitHub.
questions.explain: You install packages into a library, then load them with the (confusingly named) `library()` function.

questions.prompt: What is CRAN?
choices: The official repository of R packages, like an app store for R
The folder where R stores packages
questions.explain: CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, hosts thousands of packages that have passed quality checks.

questions.prompt: How often do you need to **install** a package?
choices: Once per computer (and again to update it)
Every time you use one of its functions
questions.explain: Install once; load with `library()` in every session.

questions.prompt: How often do you need to **load** a package with `library()`?
choices: Every R session, so at the top of every R Markdown file
Only the first time you knit
Never; R loads every installed package automatically
questions.explain: Every R session starts with no packages loaded, including the fresh session knitting starts.

questions.prompt: It's a good idea to put `install.packages("tidyverse")` at the top of your R Markdown file.
questions.explain: Knitting runs every line, so the package would be downloaded and reinstalled every time you knit. Install from the Packages tab instead.

questions.prompt: Which line loads the tidyverse correctly?
questions.explain: `library()` doesn't need quotes around the package name. `install.packages()` does.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to load the tidyverse.
questions.explain: `library()` loads an installed package into the current session.

questions.prompt: Which atomic data type stores `TRUE` or `FALSE`?
questions.explain: Logical values answer yes-or-no questions. They are written in capitals, without quotes.

questions.prompt: What does this code return?
questions.explain: The quotation marks make `"103.21"` text, even though it looks like a number.

questions.prompt: What does this code return?
questions.explain: Numbers with (or without) decimals are numeric unless you add an `L`, as in `21L`.

questions.prompt: In R, `class(21)` returns `"integer"`.
questions.explain: R stores a number you type as numeric. Add an `L` to make an integer: `class(21L)` is `"integer"`.

questions.prompt: What type is this vector?
questions.explain: A vector holds one type. Text can hold anything, so one character value coerces the whole vector to character.

questions.prompt: All the values in a vector must have the same data type.
questions.explain: A vector holds one type. Mix types and R coerces them to the one that can hold everything.

questions.prompt: Which variable name uses **snake_case**?
questions.explain: snake_case is lowercase words joined by underscores. camelCase capitalizes each word after the first.

questions.prompt: Which variable name uses **camelCase**?
questions.explain: camelCase joins words and capitalizes each word after the first.

questions.prompt: Why can't you name a variable `pop chapel hill`?
choices: Variable names must be in capitals.
Variable names can't be more than 10 letters.
questions.explain: Use camelCase or snake_case to join the words instead.

questions.prompt: Which line opens the help page for `mean()`?
questions.explain: `?mean` and `help(mean)` both open the help page in the Help tab.

questions.prompt: Which of these is **not** one of the most common mistakes students make in R?
choices: Saving files in the Downloads folder
Missing parentheses, commas, or quotation marks
questions.explain: Comments are always welcome. The other three cause most early problems.

questions.prompt: How may you use AI tools in this course?
choices: To help explain an error message, then make the fix yourself
questions.explain: AI can explain errors, but code it writes is often buggy and won't follow the course's standards.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this line?
choices: The assignment arrow points the wrong way; it should be `my_age <- 39`.
questions.explain: The name goes on the left of `<-` and the value on the right.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to load the tidyverse.
questions.explain: `library(tidyverse)`, with no quotation marks around the name.

questions.prompt: Create a logical variable `isRaining` that is `TRUE`, and a character variable `city` that holds `Chapel Hill`.
questions.explain: Logical values are written `TRUE` with no quotes; character values always go in quotes.

questions.prompt: Store the class of `21L` in a variable named `type21`.
questions.explain: `class()` returns the type as text. The `L` makes 21 an integer.

questions.prompt: `temps` was typed with one value in quotes, so `mean(temps)` doesn't work. Fix `temps` so it is numeric, then store its mean in `avg_temp`.
questions.explain: Remove the quotation marks around 68, so every value is a number. (`as.numeric(temps)` also works.)
